Thailand Lifts Temporary Export Ban on Cement; Construction Materials Firms Resume Overseas Shipments

Thailand’s Ministry of Commerce has lifted a month-long ban on cement exports, a measure that had disrupted the overseas operations of several major construction materials producers, including Siam Cement PCL/The. The decision, announced late Friday, ends a period of significant uncertainty for the industry, which relies on regional exports for a substantial portion of its revenues.

The export restriction, enacted on April 18, was introduced amid concerns over domestic supply stability as government infrastructure projects accelerated. The move, which applied to all cement products, was met with immediate concern from trade associations and industry players. According to the Thai Construction Materials Exporters Council, outbound shipments of cement plummeted by 42% in April compared to the same period last year, with an estimated value loss exceeding 2 billion baht.

“The export ban put considerable pressure on our supply chain and disrupted contractual obligations with our partners in neighboring countries,” said Natthapol Rungtaweechai, spokesperson for Siam Cement PCL/The. “We are pleased that the government has responded to industry feedback and we are now working to restore normal export volumes.”

Other affected companies, such as Eastern Concrete Solutions, reported similar impacts, with halted shipments to markets in Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar. The Construction Materials Workers’ Union warned that the export ban had led to temporary layoffs in logistics and port operations.

In announcing the end of the ban, Deputy Commerce Minister Surasak Chaisiri stated, “After reviewing domestic inventory levels and consulting with industry stakeholders, we are confident that local supply is sufficient to meet demand. Therefore, the export restriction is no longer necessary.” He noted that the government would continue to monitor the situation and could consider renewed measures if supply constraints reemerge.

Industry analysts said prompt resolution of the export ban would help restore Thailand’s reputation as a reliable supplier in the regional construction materials market. “The quick reopening of export channels is essential for maintaining the competitiveness of Thai cement brands abroad,” said Somchai Krittayapong, an analyst at the Asia-Pacific Building Materials Institute.

As of Monday, normal export operations had resumed at major shipping ports in Chonburi and Songkhla. The Thai Construction Materials Exporters Council expects May shipment volumes to rebound quickly, projecting a return to pre-ban levels by early June. Industry executives, however, cautioned that longer-term policy stability will be needed to support continued investment and growth in Thailand’s construction materials sector.
